heading: Co-op at TQM Overview
text: From January 5 to April 24, 2026, I spent four months working as a software developer at TQM through my university's Co-operative Education Program. It was my first in-depth experience working on production systems inside an enterprise engineering organization. Looking back at those four months, the experience fundamentally shifted how I approach software engineering, team collaboration, and personal growth.

heading: Stepping into the Enterprise
text: Walking into the office on day one was intimidating. Building hobby projects in isolation is completely different from contributing to a living codebase with real users, business requirements, and established infrastructure. In the beginning, I was quiet and cautious. But when you are surrounded by complex systems, you learn quickly out of necessity. Step by step, by asking questions and reviewing previous pull requests, I began finding my footing.

heading: Understanding the Real Software Engineering Lifecycle
text: Before this internship, my development workflow was simple: write code, run it locally, and push to a repository. At TQM, I experienced the complete end-to-end engineering cycle: Investigation: Breaking down business problems and understanding user pain points before writing a single line of code. Requirements & Design: Clarifying specifications, defining data contracts, and planning architecture. Implementation: Writing clean, maintainable code following team standards. Automated & Manual Testing: Ensuring unit tests pass, edge cases are covered, and regressions are caught early. User Acceptance Testing (UAT): Validating the solution with stakeholders in staging environments. Production Deployment & Monitoring: Shipping the changes safely and verifying health metrics. Experiencing this workflow firsthand taught me that writing code is often only a third of an engineer's job. Clear communication, thorough testing, and operational discipline are just as critical.

heading: Engineering Cadence and Daily Standups
text: Every morning began with a focused 15-minute standup meeting: What was completed yesterday What is planned for today Blockers, bugs, or dependencies requiring cross-team help These concise syncs kept everyone aligned and created an open environment where asking for assistance was encouraged rather than discouraged.

heading: Autonomy and Senior Mentorship
text: What I appreciated most about the engineering culture was the balance of autonomy and guidance. Developers were empowered to choose appropriate tools and patterns to solve problems effectively, keeping the focus on outcomes rather than rigid micro-management. Whenever I ran into technical hurdles, senior engineers were always willing to dive in. Instead of simply dictating the solution, they walked me through why a particular architectural choice made sense in the broader system context. Those code reviews and discussions were masterclasses in software design.

heading: Teammates and Culture
text: Navigating high-stakes releases, troubleshooting tricky regressions, and celebrating successful deployments alongside my fellow co-op interns made the journey truly memorable. We shared stress, laughter, and breakthrough moments together. Four months passed quickly, but the compound learning from real-world software development is unmatched. For any student considering a co-op or internship program: take the leap. The lessons you gain from shipping real software alongside seasoned engineers will accelerate your growth far beyond the classroom. Thank you to the entire team at TQM for an unforgettable four months.

heading: My Stack Overview
text: Here is an overview of the tools, frameworks, and services I rely on to build web applications. Software choices evolve over time, but my criteria stay consistent: developer velocity, reliability, performance, and simplicity.

heading: Next.js
text: Next.js is my primary tool for building full-stack web applications. React Server Components changed how we architect web apps by reducing client-side JavaScript, simplifying data fetching, and giving us instant access to backend resources without writing boilerplate API layers. Combined with TypeScript, it provides the best balance of speed and reliability. If I am building a production web app today, Next.js is almost always my first choice.

heading: Angular
text: When a project requires strict architectural discipline across large distributed teams, Angular is a strong contender. Its opinionated structure, built-in dependency injection, and comprehensive tooling provide consistency right out of the box.

heading: Astro
text: For content-driven websites, marketing pages, and documentation where performance is paramount, Astro excels. Its zero-JavaScript by default approach and built-in content collections make managing Markdown and MDX seamless.

heading: Node.js & Express
text: When I need a lightweight, flexible REST API or microservice in JavaScript, Express remains a dependable choice. It stays out of your way and lets you compose middleware with minimal friction.

heading: .NET & ASP.NET Core
text: For mission-critical backend services requiring enterprise-grade throughput and strict typing, ASP.NET Core with C# is exceptional. The runtime performance, native dependency injection, and asynchronous concurrency model handle high-traffic workloads effortlessly.

heading: Tailwind CSS
text: Tailwind fundamentally changed how I approach UI design. Co-locating styles directly with component markup eliminates context-switching between separate files. Thanks to the compiler, the resulting CSS bundle remains tiny and predictable.

heading: shadcn/ui
text: shadcn/ui provides accessible, beautifully crafted component primitives built on Radix UI. Because the code lives directly inside your repository rather than in an opaque node_modules package, you maintain full control over styling and behavior.

heading: Motion
text: Subtle micro-interactions and smooth layout transitions make digital interfaces feel responsive and tactile. Motion provides an intuitive declarative API to build fluid animations without degrading runtime performance.

heading: Hermes & GLM 5.3 Flash
text: AI has become an indispensable part of my daily developer workflow. Rather than relying on oversized, sluggish models, I use Hermes paired with GLM 5.3 Flash for day-to-day coding, debugging, and ideation. The combination delivers incredible inference speed, sharp reasoning, and low latency without sacrificing accuracy. It acts as an instant pair programmer—excelling at breaking down complex functions, drafting types, and answering architecture questions in real time.

heading: Vercel
text: Vercel is my default deployment target for Next.js applications. Automatic preview environments, edge routing, and zero-configuration CI/CD pipelines make deploying frictionless.

heading: AWS
text: When projects require fine-grained cloud architecture, I use AWS: CloudFront: Low-latency content delivery and edge caching worldwide. S3: Scalable, highly durable object storage for user uploads and media assets. EC2: Dedicated virtual servers when custom daemon processes or specific compute workloads are necessary.

heading: Community & Mentorship
text: Beyond writing code, I regularly organize IT workshops and volunteer for programs that help beginners and underprivileged students learn technology. Teaching concepts to others forces you to understand them deeply and helps grow the community. Great software comes from choosing tools that solve real problems, stay maintainable, and let you focus on what matters most: delivering value.

heading: Vibe Coding Overview
text: Over the past few months, I spent significant time experimenting with what many developers now call "vibe coding"—relying on large language models and prompt-driven workflows to scaffold features, resolve bugs, and iterate quickly. It is undeniable how empowering modern AI tools feel at first glance. You type a prompt describing what you want, and seconds later, a complete component or function appears on your screen. But as I leaned further into this workflow, I realized that relying solely on intuition and generative AI comes with distinct tradeoffs that every developer needs to recognize.

heading: The Illusion of Instant Velocity
text: When you prompt your way through an entire project without inspecting the generated code, your initial velocity skyrockets. You bypass reading documentation, you skip debugging with breakpoints, and you avoid wrestling with tricky edge cases. However, speed without comprehension is fragile. When you delegate all problem-solving to an AI model, you gradually lose touch with how your application actually functions. When a subtle state bug or memory leak inevitably happens in production, you find yourself unable to debug code you never truly understood in the first place. If you do not read and comprehend the code you commit, you are not developing software—you are simply outsourcing your judgment. True engineering is not just about outputting lines of code; it is about building mental models of how systems interact, fail, and scale.

heading: Reframing AI as an Accelerated Learning Partner
text: The real breakthrough came when I shifted how I interact with AI. Instead of using it as a ghostwriter to blindly generate code, I began treating it as an interactive pair-programmer and research assistant. When encountering unfamiliar libraries or complex algorithms, ask questions that challenge both the model and your understanding: Why is this specific pattern or data structure recommended here? What are the performance implications and potential memory bottlenecks? Can you explain how this function behaves when network conditions fail? What are alternative architectural approaches and their tradeoffs? When used this way, AI transforms into a tireless tutor. It compresses the time required to understand complex concepts and encourages you to read official documentation with deeper curiosity.

heading: Principles I Follow When Coding with AI
text: Read before committing: Always trace every execution path, check variable scopes, and verify error boundaries before merging code into your branch. Own the architecture: Use AI for boilerplate and exploratory snippets, but keep ownership of data flow, domain models, and high-level system design. Document what you learn: Take active notes on new patterns, APIs, and edge cases you discover during each session. Turning fleeting insights into written knowledge cements your skills. Tools will continue to evolve, but the fundamentals of problem solving, disciplined curiosity, and clear thinking remain irreplaceable.

JavaScript Closures
text:
A closure is a function bundled together with references to its lexical environment, allowing it to access outer variables even after the outer function has executed.

### Closures & Lexical Scoping

A closure gives an inner function persistent access to its outer enclosing scope, even after the outer function returns.

```javascript
function createCounter(initialValue = 0) {
  let count = initialValue; // Private variable encapsulated in closure
  return {
    increment: () => ++count,
    decrement: () => --count,
    get: () => count,
  };
}

const counter = createCounter(10);
console.log(counter.increment()); // 11
console.log(counter.increment()); // 12
console.log(counter.get());       // 12
```

**Why this matters in modern development:**
- **Data Encapsulation:** Emulates private state without class fields.
- **Factory Functions & Currying:** Enables reusable, parameterized functions.
- **React Hooks Architecture:** Hooks like `useState` and `useEffect` fundamentally rely on closures over render scopes.

Strict (===) vs Loose (==) Equality
text:
Loose equality (==) performs implicit type coercion according to complex abstract equality rules, while strict equality (===) checks value and type without conversion.

### Equality & Type Coercion

Loose equality (`==`) invokes the Abstract Equality Comparison algorithm, leading to notorious counter-intuitive results:

```javascript
0 == false        // true
'' == false       // true
[] == false       // true
null == undefined // true
null === undefined// false (different types)
```

**Production Rule:** Always use `===` (strict equality) and `!==` to avoid unintentional implicit coercion bugs.

heading: Variable Declarations & Scoping
text:
var is function-scoped and hoisted with undefined initialization. let and const are block-scoped with a Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ). Prefer const by default, let when reassigning.

### Scoping: var vs let vs const

| Feature | `var` | `let` | `const` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scope | Function | Block `{}` | Block `{}` |
| Hoisting | Initialized to `undefined` | Temporal Dead Zone (Error) | Temporal Dead Zone (Error) |
| Reassignable | Yes | Yes | No (Reference is locked) |

```javascript
// const locks the binding, not mutation of object contents:
const person = { name: 'Alex' };
person.name = 'Sam'; //  Valid mutation
// person = {};           //  TypeError
```

ES Modules (ESM) vs CommonJS (CJS)
text:
ES Modules use static declarative import/export syntax analyzed at compile time, enabling tree-shaking and browser support. CommonJS is runtime dynamic loading historically used in Node.

### Module Systems: ESM vs CJS

- **ESM (ECMAScript Modules):**
  - Syntax: `import x from 'x'`, `export default x`
  - Static analysis: bundlers can prune unused code (tree-shaking).
  - Native in browsers and modern Node.js runtimes (Bun, Node 18+).
- **CommonJS (CJS):**
  - Syntax: `const x = require('x')`, `module.exports = x`
  - Dynamic at runtime: cannot easily be tree-shaken.

Virtual DOM & React Reconciliation
text:
React maintains an in-memory Virtual DOM tree. When state changes, reconciliation computes the minimal diff against the previous tree to surgically mutate the real DOM.

### Virtual DOM & React Fiber

1. **Render Phase:** Evaluates JSX components and generates a virtual DOM tree (pure, interruptible by Fiber in concurrent mode).
2. **Reconciliation:** Diffs the new tree against the old tree using heuristics (e.g. `key` attributes).
3. **Commit Phase:** Synchronously updates the real browser DOM with minimal DOM mutations.

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)
text:
CORS is a browser security mechanism that restricts cross-origin HTTP requests unless the server explicitly grants permission via HTTP response headers.

### CORS & Browser Security

Browsers enforce the Same-Origin Policy (Protocol + Domain + Port). When fetching across origins:
1. **Simple Requests (GET/POST with standard headers):** Sent directly; browser blocks reading response if `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is missing.
2. **Preflighted Requests (PUT, DELETE, custom headers like Bearer):** Browser first sends an `OPTIONS` request to ask server permissions before executing the actual request.

heading: JWT (JSON Web Tokens) & Secure Auth
text:
JWTs are compact, cryptographically signed tokens containing claims. Best stored in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies to mitigate XSS and CSRF risks.

### JSON Web Tokens (JWT)

A JWT contains 3 base64url-encoded parts separated by dots:
`Header.Payload.Signature`

- **Header:** Algorithm & token type (e.g., HS256, RS256).
- **Payload:** User claims (e.g., `userId`, `role`, `exp`).
- **Signature:** Hash of Header + Payload verified by the server's private secret.

**Security Best Practice:** Store auth tokens in `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax/Strict` cookies. Storing sensitive JWTs in `localStorage` exposes them to XSS exfiltration.

heading: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) Defense
text:
XSS occurs when malicious scripts are injected into trusted websites. Mitigated by context-aware escaping, Content Security Policy (CSP), and avoiding unsafe innerHTML injections.

### XSS Prevention Strategies

1. **Auto-Escaping:** React automatically escapes values embedded in JSX expressions `{userInput}`.
2. **Avoid Unsafe Injection:** Strictly avoid `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` unless sanitized with DOMPurify.
3. **Content Security Policy (CSP):** Restrict executable script sources in HTTP response headers.
4. **Cookie Flags:** Mark session cookies as `HttpOnly` so JavaScript cannot read session tokens even if an XSS flaw exists.

heading: React 19 New Features
text:
React 19 introduces the React Compiler for automatic memoization, Actions and async form handling, the new use hook, Server Components, and native document metadata.

### React 19 Overview

React 19 brings foundational improvements to frontend development:

- **React Compiler**: An automatic optimizing compiler that analyzes JavaScript semantics to memoize computations and components automatically, eliminating manual `useMemo` and `useCallback`.
- **Actions & Async Transitions**: Native support for handling async functions in transitions, with automatic pending states, optimistic updates, and error handling.
- **New Hooks**:
  - `useActionState`: Manages async action lifecycle with pending flags and return values.
  - `useFormStatus`: Allows child form components to read parent form submission status without prop drilling.
  - `useOptimistic`: Manages optimistic UI updates while async operations resolve.
- **The `use` Hook**: Dynamically reads resources like promises and context during render, including conditional usage inside loops and if-statements.
- **Native Document Metadata**: Built-in support for `<title>`, `<meta>`, and stylesheet link tags directly in components with automatic hoisting to `<head>`.
- **Server Components & Server Actions**: Stable, first-class primitives for running server-only code with zero client bundle impact.

heading: Angular Framework
text:
Angular suits projects needing strict architectural discipline across large teams: opinionated structure, built-in dependency injection, and comprehensive tooling.

### Angular Framework

When a project requires strict architectural discipline across large distributed teams, Angular is a strong contender. Its opinionated structure, built-in dependency injection, and comprehensive tooling provide consistency right out of the box.

Reach for Angular when many teams must ship consistently against shared conventions; reach for React when you want a smaller core with a pick-your-own ecosystem.

heading: Web Accessibility (a11y)
text: Inclusive web design ensuring semantic HTML, proper contrast, keyboard navigability, and ARIA landmarks for screen readers.

heading: Semantic HTML
text: Using tags like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, and <section> to provide meaningful structural hierarchy for browsers, screen readers, and search crawlers.

heading: Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
text: Generating HTML on the server dynamically per request. Improves first contentful paint and ensures full search engine indexing.

heading: Static Site Generation (SSG)
text: Compiling pages to static HTML at build time, served directly via global CDNs for minimal latency and cost.

heading: Hydration
text: The browser phase where React attaches event listeners and runtime state to pre-rendered HTML received from the server.

heading: Tailwind CSS
text: A utility-first CSS framework enabling rapid composition of design systems directly within JSX markup with zero runtime overhead.

heading: Zustand
text: A lightweight, un-opinionated state management library for React using simple hooks without boilerplate context providers.

heading: tRPC
text: End-to-end type safety between client and server without code generation by sharing TypeScript type definitions directly.

heading: CI/CD Pipelines
text: Automated continuous integration (testing, linting) and continuous deployment workflows (e.g. GitHub Actions, Vercel) that validate and ship code reliably.

heading: Memoization
text: An optimization technique that caches the return values of expensive pure functions keyed by input parameters.
